text:
IN
THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Saed v. Wittenberg,

2010 BCSC 910

Date: 20100628

Docket:
S076586

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

Vian Saed

Plaintiff

And

Dr. Gerald Wittenberg and
Dr. Gerald Wittenberg Inc.

Defendants

Before: The Honourable Madam Justice Ross

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Plaintiff:

Jonas Dubas

Counsel for the Defendants:

Mark
M. Skorah, Q.C.

Stacey E. Grubb

Place and Date of Hearing:

Vancouver, B.C.

June 4, 2010

Place and Date of Judgment:

Vancouver, B.C.

June 28, 2010

[
1
]

This is an application brought by the defendants
pursuant to Rule 19(24) for an order to strike paragraphs 12, 18(c) and 18(d)
from the Statement of Claim. The plaintiff alleges that the defendant,
Dr. Wittenberg, negligently provided medical and/or dental advice and
negligently performed medical and/or dental surgical services between May 31,
2005 and February 23, 2007 in his capacity as an oral surgeon.

[
2
]

The pleadings at issue provide:

12.       The Plaintiff states that prior to
becoming the physician of the Plaintiff Wittenberg was the subject of prior
legal proceedings, both in the Supreme Court of British Columbia and with the
College of Dental Surgeons and these proceedings involved both founded and
unfounded complaints from Wittenberg’s prior patients respecting the negligent
provision of medical, surgical and dental advice to these patients and/or
negligent performance of medical, dental, and/or surgical procedures on these
patients, and as such, the Plaintiff states that Wittenberg knew or should have
known that he was not competent to provide the Plaintiff with advice respecting
the medical, dental, and surgical procedures he performed on July 28, 2006 or
to perform any or some of the procedures that he performed on the Plaintiff
and/or that he failed to seek any remedial training, to correct prior problems
respecting any such professional deficiencies and Wittenberg is therefore
responsible to the Plaintiff for, not only general and special damages, but
also increased, aggravated, and punitive damages.

...

18(c)    Failing to recognize, given the
prior founded and unfounded complaints made against Wittenberg with respect to
the dental college or legal proceedings undertaken in court formally or outside
of the court process by prior patients, that Wittenberg was not qualified to
advise the Plaintiff or perform any of the medical or surgical procedures he
performed upon the Plaintiff;

18(d)    Failing
to take proper and/or any corrective measures with respect to his training and
expertise, prior to operating on the Plaintiff, to correct any of the
deficiencies in his abilities, which should have been apparent to him as
necessary to, correct any of the issues outlined in paragraph 18(c) hereto;

[
3
]

The defendants submit that the plaintiff is
seeking to establish that Dr. Wittenberg is liable based upon peer reviews
and court decisions in relation to past conduct involving other patients that
have nothing to do with his treatment of the plaintiff or the negligence
alleged in relation to his treatment of the plaintiff. There is no evidence of
specific or pervasive problems. The pleadings are, in the defendants’
submission, a veiled attempt to engage in a fishing expedition. As such, the
defendants submit the paragraphs at issue do not disclose a cause of action,
nor do they plead material facts upon which to base a cause of action. They are
unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous and vexatious. They will result in delay of
a fair trial and constitute an abuse of process.

[
4
]

The plaintiff submits that the pleadings are
necessary to deal with the claim for aggravated and punitive damages and to
prove negligence through similar fact evidence. The plaintiff submits further
that prior actions and complaints, both founded and unfounded, are relevant
because they should have caused Dr. Wittenberg to realize that he should
not have been undertaking cosmetic surgery or that he should have undertaken
remedial training. Thus, counsel submits, the prior complaints even if
unfounded are directly relevant to the alleged breach of duty to the plaintiff.
The plaintiff submits that it is premature to strike the pleadings because
until document disclosure and examinations for discovery are complete, the
plaintiff cannot particularize the conduct.

[
5
]

Rule 19(24) provides:

(24)      At any stage of a proceeding the
court may order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of an
endorsement, pleading, petition or other document on the ground that

(a)        it discloses no reasonable claim or defence as the case
may be,

(b)        it is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

(c)        it may prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or
hearing or the proceeding, or

(d)        it is otherwise an abuse of the process of the court,

and the court may grant judgment or order
the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and may order the costs of the
application to be paid as special costs.

[
6
]

For the purpose of an application pursuant to
Rule 19(24)(a), the sole question is whether, assuming that all the facts
alleged by the plaintiff are true, the plaintiff can present a question “fit to
be tried”. It must be “plain and obvious” that the statement of claim discloses
no reasonable cause of action, see
Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc.
,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2
S.C.R. 959.

[
7
]

Guidelines in determining whether it is “plain and
obvious” that the plaintiff’s case discloses no reasonable cause of action
include the following factors:

(a)       Whether there is a question fit to be tried regardless of
complexity or novelty;

(b)       Whether the outcome is beyond a reasonable doubt;

(c)        Whether serious questions of law or of general importance
are raised or facts should be known before trial;

(d)       Whether the pleadings can be amended; and

(e)       Whether there is an element of abuse of process, see
Midwest
Management (1987) Ltd. v. British Columbia Gas Utility Ltd.

(1997), 34
C.L.R. (2d) 186 (B.C.S.C.)
and
Owners, Strata Plan LMS 1328 v. Surrey (City
of)
,
2001 BCCA 693
, 95 B.C.L.R. (3d) 315 at para.
5
.

[
8
]

The meaning of the terms used in subrules
19(24)(b) and (c) was discussed by Romilly J. in
Citizens for Foreign Aid
Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
(1999),
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C. (4th) 266
(B.C.S.C.) at para.
47
:

[47]      Irrelevancy
and embarrassment are both established when pleadings are so confusing that it
is difficult to understand what is being pleaded:
Gittings v. Caneco
Audio-Publishers Inc.
(1987),
1987 CanLII 2561 (BC SC)
, 17 B.C.L.R. (2d) 38 (B.C.S.C.). An
“embarrassing” and “scandalous” pleading is one that is so irrelevant that it
will involve the parties in useless expense and will prejudice the trial of the
action by involving them in a dispute apart from the issues:
Keddie v. Dumas
Hotels Ltd. (Cariboo Trail Hotel)
(1985),
1985 CanLII 417 (BC CA)
, 62 B.C.L.R. 145 (B.C.C.A.) at
147. An allegation which is scandalous will not be struck if it is relevant to
the proceedings. It will only be struck if irrelevant as well as scandalous:

College of Dental Surgeons (British Columbia) v. Cleland
(1968),
1968 CanLII 1008 (BC CA)
, 66 W.W.R.
499 (B.C.C.A.). A pleading is “unnecessary” or “vexatious” if it does not go to
establishing the plaintiff’s cause of action or does not advance any claim
known in law:
Strauts v. Harrigan
(December 2, 1991), Doc. Vancouver
C913631 (B.C.S.C.). A pleading that is superfluous will not be struck out if it
is not necessarily unnecessary or otherwise objectionable:
Lutz

v.
Canadian Puget Sound Lumber and Timber Co.

(1920), 28 B.C.R 39 (B.C.C.A.)
.
A pleading is “frivolous” if it is obviously unsustainable, not in the sense
that it lacks an evidentiary basis, but because of the doctrine of estoppel:
Chrisgian
v. B.C. Rail Ltd.
(July 3, 1992), Doc. Prince George 20714 (B.C. Master).

[
9
]

The doctrine of abuse of process was discussed
by Garson J., as she then was, in
Dempsey v. Envision Credit Union
,
2006
BCSC 750
, supplementary reasons at
2006 BCSC 1324
[
Dempsey
]:

[9]        Pleadings will be struck out if
they abuse the process of the court. Abuse of process is a flexible doctrine
that allows the court to prevent a claim from proceeding where it “violates
such principles as judicial economy, consistency, finality and the integrity of
the administration of justice”. (see
Toronto (City) v. Canadian Union of
Public Employees (CUPE) Local 79
,
2003 SCC 63 (CanLII)
, [2003] 3 S.C.R. 77 at ¶
37
).

[10]      One way in which these principles
are violated is where parties make allegations in subsequent proceedings that
are
res judicata
. Parties may not bring forward in a subsequent action,
points related to the subject matter of previous litigation that the parties,
exercising reasonable diligence, might have been able to bring forward. (
Johnson
v. Gore Wood & Co.
,
2002 2 A.C.1 at 23
English Court of Appeal and
Samos
Investments Inc. v. Pattison
,
[2004] B.C.J. No. 705
).

...

[12]      In
Babavic
v. Babowech
,
[1993] B.C.J. No. 1802 (S.C.) at ¶ 18
it was held that R.
19(24)(d) gives the court the discretion to dismiss actions on the basis of
abuse of process, that is, where the court process is being used for an
improper purpose:

The categories of abuse of process are
open. Abuse of process may be found where proceedings involve a deception on
the court or constitute a mere sham; where the process of the court is not
being fairly or honestly used, or is employed for some ulterior or improper
purpose; proceeding which are without foundation or serve no useful purpose and
multiple or successive readings which cause or are likely to cause vexation or
oppression.

[
10
]

In
Dempsey
, Garson J. extracted the
following general propositions from the authorities concerning the
circumstances under which pleadings will be struck:

[17]      In summary, a pleading will be
struck out if:

(a)        the
pleadings are unintelligible, confusing and difficult to understand (
Citizens
for Foreign [A]id Reform, supra
);

(b)        the
pleadings do not establish a cause of action and do not advance a claim known
in law (
Citizens for Foreign [A]id Reform, supra
);

(c)        the
pleadings are without substance in that they are groundless, fanciful and
trifle with the Court’s time (
Borsato v. Basra
[,
2000 BCSC 28
, rev’d on
other grounds
2000 BCSC 1898
])

(d)        the
pleadings are not bona fides, are oppressive and are designed to cause the
Defendants anxiety, trouble and expense
(
Borsato v. Basra
, supra
);

(e)        the action is brought for an
improper purpose, particularly the harassment and oppression of the Defendants
(
Ebrahim v. Ebrahim
,
2002 BCSC 466
).

[
11
]

The plaintiff cited the following authorities in
support of the position she takes with respect to the pleadings
D.M.M. v.
Pilo
,
[1996] O.J. No. 938 (Gen. Div.) [
Pilo
]
is a decision at
trial. The plaintiff’s claims in
Pilo
included breach of fiduciary duty
related to a pattern of sexual assaults, emotional and psychological abuse
perpetrated by the physician over a period of 11 years. The pleadings do not
appear to contain any allegations similar to those at issue in the present
case. The plaintiff did rely upon similar fact evidence at trial. The reasons
make reference to a striking pattern of common characteristics to the
plaintiffs’ allegations. Punitive damages were awarded.

[
12
]

I did not find this case of assistance with respect
to the present application. There were apparently no similar pleadings to those
in the present case. The defendants in the present case do not contend that
punitive damages would not be available in an appropriate case, nor that
similar fact evidence would never be admissible at trial. It is clear that the
similar fact evidence relied upon in
Pilo
bore striking similarities.
There is no such allegation in the present case.

[
13
]

Sinclair v. March
,

2000 BCSC 349
, 73 B.C.L.R. (3d) 86, varied
2000 BCCA 459
, was an application
concerning document disclosure. The plaintiff sought records of other patients
who had undergone the same surgical procedure to rebut the defendant’s
assertion that he always performed the procedure in a particular way with no
complications. The plaintiff sought such evidence to establish that the
procedure was inherently dangerous, that the failure rate was higher than that
disclosed in the informed consent and as similar fact evidence. The Statement
of Claim alleged failure to obtain informed consent, failure to discontinue the
procedure once the serious risk was known and negligent performance and after
care. At paras. 32-3 Dillon J. addressed similar fact evidence as follows:

...The probative value of such
documents arises within the rule as to similar facts which allows the
introduction of such evidence when the acts are so strikingly similar that the
similarity is not attributable to coincidence (
R. v. C.(M.H.)
,
1991 CanLII 94 (SCC)
,
[1991] 1 S.C.R. 763
;

4 C.R. (4th) 1
at 7
(S.C.C.);
Doe v. Hirt
, (14 September 1993), Vancouver C911766 (B.C.S.C.)).
The evidence must be so similar that it would tend to prove some fact essential
to the plaintiff's case. In
Chong v. Royal Columbian Hospital
,
[1996] B.C.J. No. 1364
;
(18 June 1996), Vancouver C953391 (B.C.S.C.), this was described at para. 17
as requiring a "nexus apparent to an issue in the action the person is
being examined upon".

The
fact that the same procedure was performed upon others is certainly
insufficiently relevant to require production of these documents. However, the
plaintiff says that the evidence relates to complication rates and knowledge of
serious risks. Thus, there may be relevance to the pleading of lack of
disclosure of risks in informed consent and continuation of the risky procedure
once known. The plaintiff's restriction of the request to patients with the
same procedure performed who also suffered the post-operative complication of
peritonitis creates the nexus apparent to the issue as plead, notwithstanding
that the particulars of the plaintiff's complications have not been plead.

In the present case there is no such
“striking similarity” or apparent nexus.

[
14
]

Williams v. Wai-Ping

(2005), 27 C.P.C. (6th) 83 (Ont. S.C.J.)
was an application that
concerned a motion to strike paragraphs from the Statement of Claim that made
reference to other actions on the basis that the allegations were scandalous,
frivolous and vexatious , pleaded impermissible similar fact evidence and
disclosed no cause of action. In concluding that the decision of the case
management judge to permit the pleading to stand was correct, the court cited
the decision of Epstein J. in
Garwood Financial Ltd. v. Wallace
(1997),

1997 CanLII 12276 (ON CTGD)
, 35 O.R. (3d) 280 (Gen. Div.), which held that in considering whether similar
facts may be pleaded the court is to weigh the added complexity against the
potential probative value. The court also cited with approval the factors
identified in
Prism Data Services Ltd. v. Neopost Inc
.,
[2003] O.J.
No. 2994
as follows at para. 11:

He then adopted the factors enumerated by Master Egan in
Prism
Data Services Lid. v. Neopost Inc
.,
[2003] O.J. No. 2994

(Ont. Master)
as the relevant principles to apply when a party seeks to plead
allegations of similar facts. They are:

(a)         Such
allegations are proper as long as the added complexity resulting therefrom does
not outweigh the probative value;

(b)         Similar
acts are not probative if there is not a sufficient degree of similarity;

(c)         The
similarity must be provable without prolonged inquiry, although inevitably, the
litigation process will be lengthened to some extent as a result of proper
similar fact allegations;

(d)         The
added complexity should not lead to undue oppression or unfairness;

(e)         If a
system or scheme of conduct is alleged, the past similar acts must have
sufficient common features to constitute the system or scheme.

[
15
]

In the present case there is no particularity
provided by which the court could conclude whether there was a sufficient
degree of similarity. The pleading is very broad, encompassing founded and
unfounded claims with no limitation with respect to the nature of the claim.

[
16
]

I have concluded that for all the reasons cited
by the defendants in their submissions, the paragraphs at issue cannot stand in
their present form. They do not conform to the requirements for pleading
similar facts. There is no nexus to the procedure performed upon the plaintiff.
In my view these deficiencies are not saved by the addition of a claim for
punitive damages.

[
17
]

In the result, there will be an order:

(a)       striking
paragraph 12 of the Statement of Claim;

(b)       striking the phrase “given the prior founded and unfounded
complaints made against Wittenberg with respect to the dental college or legal
proceedings undertaken in court formally or outside of the court process by
prior patients” from paragraph 18(c) of the Statement of Claim; and

(c)        striking
the phrase “which should have been apparent to him as necessary to correct any
of the issues outlined in paragraph 18(c) hereto”.

“Ross J.”
